passage: Suraj, why do I ask before I say no to your phone? Let me tell you about my daughter Sunaina. I'm Vikas, your uncle. She was eleven, chatting with an assistant on the family tablet, and I got worried and asked to see. Her face went stiff. "You don't trust me," she said, and I felt awful, because that wasn't it. I told her I was nervous, not angry. She turned the tablet toward me. She used it for spelling games and questions about frogs. We sat on the sofa and made three rules together: no giving out our address, tell me if anything feels strange, and no chatting at bedtime. Funny thing, after that she started showing me things without being asked.

qa.q: What did Sunaina use the assistant for?
qa.a: She used it for spelling games and questions about frogs.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina say, "You don't trust me"?
qa.a: She felt watched and hurt when her father asked to see her chats, and her stiff face showed it.

qa.q: What made the sharing work for Sunaina and Vikas?
qa.a: She showed him openly, he explained he was nervous rather than angry, and together they made three rules.

qa.q: What was it like for Vikas when Sunaina said he did not trust her?
qa.a: He felt awful, because asking came from his nervousness and not from anger.

grounding: A parent's worry leads a child to feel watched, then to share openly and agree rules together.
